content: Xanthine oxidase is an enzyme that catalyzes the sequential oxidation of hypoxanthine and xanthine, ultimately leading to the production of uric acid, which is the end product of human purine metabolism. Inhibiting xanthine oxidase not only reduces uric acid production but also results in increased levels of hypoxanthine and xanthine. While xanthine cannot be converted into purine ribotides, hypoxanthine can be salvaged into the purine ribotides adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). Elevated levels of these ribotides may lead to feedback inhibition of amidophosphoribosyl transferase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme in purine biosynthesis. Consequently, allopurinol reduces uric acid formation and may also inhibit purine synthesis. Allopurinol is chemically known as 1,5-dihydro-4H-pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidin-4-one. It functions as a xanthine oxidase inhibitor and is administered orally. Each scored white to off-white tablet contains 100 mg of allopurinol along with inactive ingredients such as lactose monohydrate, corn starch, sodium starch glycolate, povidone, and stearic acid. Each scored peach-colored tablet contains 300 mg of allopurinol and includes the same inactive ingredients, with the addition of FD&C Yellow No. 6. There is limited information available regarding the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of allopurinol tablets in the drug label. Additionally, the FDA package insert for allopurinol does not provide details on clinical studies. Allopurinol tablets are supplied in the following forms: 100 mg white to off-white, round, beveled-edged, uncoated tablets embossed with RG 10 on one side and a breakline on the other. These are available in bottles of 100 tablets (NDC 63304-539-01) and 1000 tablets (NDC 63304-539-10). 300 mg peach-colored, round, beveled-edged, uncoated tablets embossed with RG 11 on one side and a breakline on the other. These are available in bottles of 100 tablets (NDC 63304-540-01) and 500 tablets (NDC 63304-540-05). The recommended storage conditions for allopurinol tablets are at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Patients should be informed of the following precautions: 1. Discontinue allopurinol tablets and consult a physician immediately if they experience a skin rash, painful urination, blood in the urine, eye irritation, or swelling of the lips or mouth. 2. Continue therapy as prescribed for gouty attacks, as the optimal benefit of allopurinol may take 2 to 6 weeks to manifest. 3. Increase fluid intake during therapy to prevent the formation of renal stones. 4. If a dose is missed, it should not be doubled at the next scheduled time. 5. Be aware of potential risks associated with the concomitant use of allopurinol and medications such as dicumarol, sulfinpyrazone, mercaptopurine, azathioprine, ampicillin, amoxicillin, and thiazide diuretics, and follow the physician's instructions. 6. Due to the occasional occurrence of drowsiness, patients should exercise caution when engaging in activities requiring alertness. 7. Taking allopurinol tablets after meals may help minimize gastric irritation. The interaction between alcohol and allopurinol has not been established. Patients should consult their physician regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication. Allopurinol is marketed under the brand name Zyloprim. There is limited information available regarding look-alike drug names.
